 Manhattan Embraces Diwali From Times Square to Federal Hall 
 Manhattan celebrated Diwali with festivities across the borough, bringing South Asian culture, food and traditions to some of New York City’s most recognizable landmarks. With the Festival of Lights falling on Nov. 8, celebrations continued in the days that followed. 
 Christian Spencer | 15 Nov 2026 | 11:54

 Photo: Kundan Adhikari )
 Friends in embroidered sherwanis and formal wear share animated conversation and cocktails beneath the soaring classical architecture at Federal Hall. (
 Photo: Kundan Adhikari )

 Photo: Kundan Adhikari )

 Photo: Raúl Larsen / RGBTV Photography )
 A floral rosy cocktail, topped with dried rose petals, a citrus wheel, and a fresh carnation, brings extra color and fragrance from Kismat to Federal Hall. (
 Photo: Christian Spencer )
 A chili-rimmed cocktail from garnished with a dried lime and orchid flower adds a colorful touch, from Kismat. (
 Photo: Christian Spencer )
 The historic rotunda of Federal Hall National Memorial comes alive with purple light, music, and celebration as guests gather for Diwali, with DJ Axar spinning and the landmark’s iconic columns and eagle overlooking the festive scene. (
 Photo: Raúl Larsen/ RGBTV Photography )
 A young violinist performs in a soft pink silk sari, adding live classical music to the Diwali festivities at Federal Hall. (

 South Asian communities in Brooklyn, Queens and Jersey City continue to mark Diwali feast in households and temples, but Manhattan has emerged as the city’s most prominent destination for the Festival of Lights, marking the triumph of light over darkness.
 While the holiday itself fell on Nov. 8 this year, the celebrations function more like a weeklong season, with several Manhattan events taking place both before and after the official date.
 New York City public schools have closed for Diwali since 2023, following legislation signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul. While it is not a federal holiday, the observance has taken root in the city’s cultural calendar. Mayor Zohran Mamdani marked the occasion this year with public greetings and a video celebration of the city’s diversity, continuing a tradition of mayoral involvement that included Gracie Mansion events in prior years.
 Two gatherings this season captured both the scale and intimacy of the moment.
 On Oct. 24, the 11th annual Diwali at Times Square transformed Broadway between 46th and 48th Streets into a sea of color, music and light. Diwali at Times Square continues to draw large crowds even in harsh weather, with attendees remaining committed to the live performances and festive activities even when the event is postponed. Organizers described it as the largest Diwali festival outside India. Crowds packed the plaza for performances, a bazaar, a kids zone and a ceremonial diya lighting synchronized with the One Times Square tower countdown.
 For many attendees, the public setting felt surprisingly personal.
 Anjali Patel, attending for the first time, said the event transported her. “It was like we are at home. We are in India,” she said. “It feels like one family to us. And I’ve never imagined playing Bollywood songs at Times Square.”
 Prerna Saini, who has lived in New York for six years, described a more emotional reaction. “Today, it feels like literally I got goosebumps, because I’m too far away from my family,” she said. “It feels like all the way family... It’s bringing all the culture together. That’s why I love New York and Times Square.”
 Tanishka Chauhan, who lives on Roosevelt Island, came to compare the public celebration with her family’s traditions. She wanted to see how the city portrayed “such a beautiful religious event.” Her takeaway reached beyond the South Asian community: “Diversity, inclusion, and learning about other cultures is one of the biggest things I want people to take away from this event. I love everybody’s culture, and I want people to love my culture as well.”
 Two weeks later, on Nov. 6, a more intimate gathering filled Federal Hall downtown for the first-ever Diwali at Federal Hall. Hosted by Pankti Doshi—best known for her five-day wedding that included a permitted parade on Fifth Avenue—in her fifth year organizing the event, the celebration drew community members, creators and small business owners.
 The Federal Hall celebration functioned like a Desi party. Everyday South Asian New Yorkers shared a glamorous moment dancing, singing and dining on traditional bite-sized meals and sweets provided by Desi Galli, a well-respected restaurant and catering company, with founder Chef Pria Vanda attending the event.
 Meema Agarwal, who grew up in a homogeneous state, said the public recognition felt transformative. “Living in New York City, seeing it being recognized, seeing so many people celebrating, is amazing,” she said. “Diwali is a vibrant, beautiful holiday, and you don’t have to be Indian to be able to appreciate and enjoy it.”
 Model Slesha Patel, originally from Kansas, noted the contrast with her hometown. She traditionally focused on religious pujas with her grandmother and found herself drawn into the social side this year. “It’s really nice to see New York City as a whole embracing Diwali. It’s nice to see brands embracing Diwali,” she said. “Where I’m from in Kansas, that’s not nearly as common.”
 Her companion, business school student Shikha Patel, emphasized visibility. The celebrations, she said, make the festival “more visible externally to non-South Asian people” and show that “Diwali can be celebrated by everyone and anyone.”
 Content creator Sreya Nagumalla, who recently moved to New York, called the Federal Hall night meaningful because of its inclusive spirit. “I want people to take away that there’s an inclusive community, no matter how big you are, if you’re a creator, if you’re a model, famous or not,” she said. “There is a space for you in such a big city, and it can feel like a very small circle once you meet the people that respect you within your circle.”
 Akeema Francis, who launched her bar and cocktail consultation business in June, saw practical opportunity in the growing recognition. She provides signature drinks and décor for celebrations and predicted more public events. “Hopefully in the future, we can see block parties and things of that nature,” she said. For her, Diwali centers on “coming together... good drinks, good food.”
 Neha Multani (Miss India New York 2007), who works in IT and manages a jewelry business, kept her message simple: attendees should leave understanding “how colorful a culture is.”
 New Yorkers can continue celebrating Diwali after Nov. 8 with a free event at the South Street Seaport Museum on Nov. 10 from 4 to 6 p.m.
 The Manhattan celebration, organized with The Culture Tree , will feature diya decorating, puppet storytelling, henna and an interactive dance workshop set to Diwali music.
 The family-friendly event is intended for children ages 5 and older and will take place at 12 Fulton St. in Lower Manhattan.
 The NYPD also marked the holiday with its third annual Diwali Heritage & Cultural Celebration at One Police Plaza on Nov. 10, bringing together South Asian officers, community leaders and cultural organizations, including the NYPD Desi Society and Indian Officers’ Society.
 Police Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch attended the celebration and later wrote on X , “Diwali is also a time to celebrate our traditions, strengthen our relationships, and come together as a community,” while thanking the participating organizations for recognizing the holiday. The event also featured traditional diya lighting and cultural performances, with Certified IT Administrator Srujal Parikh receiving an Award for Exceptional Service to New York City.
 “Diwali is a vibrant, beautiful holiday, and you don’t have to be Indian to be able to appreciate and enjoy it.” Meema Agarwal at Times Square celebration Facebook
